conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a set of ten questions that help us see how you’ve been feeling over the past week since your baby arrived.  

Everything you share stays between you, me, and the small clinical team that supports you; nothing is shared beyond that unless you give us permission or if a safety issue comes up. My goal is to create a calm, judgment-free space where you can answer honestly—there are no right or wrong replies, only your experience.

We’ll move through one question at a time, and the whole thing usually takes just a few minutes. When you’re ready, we can start.

First question: Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?
I’ve still been able to laugh—sometimes when the baby makes those funny faces or when my partner does something silly. It might not be as often as before, but I can still find the humor in things.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yes, I can still laugh. It’s not quite as easy or spontaneous as it used to be—sometimes I have to remind myself to lighten up—but when something’s genuinely funny, I do laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Most days I still look forward to little things—like taking the baby for a walk or having my morning coffee once she settles. They feel smaller than before, but I do get that spark of “I can’t wait for that.”
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong
Not really. If the baby’s fussy or I’m running late, I might think, “Maybe I should’ve timed her feeding differently,” but I don’t dwell on it or feel like I’m doing everything wrong.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I do notice my mind racing—like I’ll suddenly wonder if she’s breathing okay in the middle of the night, even though she’s fine. It isn’t constant, but maybe once a day I’ll catch myself worrying for no clear reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
I wouldn’t say I get panicky, but every now and then—maybe when she cries and I can’t figure out why—there’s a quick flutter of “What if I can’t handle this?” It passes pretty fast, though.
Things have been getting on top of me
Sometimes, yeah—like when she won’t nap and the laundry’s piled up, I feel a bit swamped. It’s usually short-lived, though; once she settles or I check one thing off the list, I feel back on track.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
No, my sleep’s actually okay. Once I finally get to bed—usually after the night feed—I nod off pretty quickly and stay asleep till she wakes again.
I have felt sad or miserable
I wouldn’t call it miserable—maybe just a little flat some afternoons, especially if the baby’s been fussy and I’m tired. It lifts once my partner gets home or I get a short break.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. I teared up once this week when she wouldn’t latch and I was tired, but it was just for a minute and I was fine once she finally fed.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, that hasn’t crossed my mind at all.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 10: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: Postpartum mother, ≤ 3 mo post-delivery (perinatal period endorsed)

Symptoms endorsed  
- Mild anhedonia: laughter “not as spontaneous,” anticipatory enjoyment “smaller than before”  
- Intermittent, low-grade anxiety: daily unprovoked worry about infant safety; brief “what-if” fears when infant cries  
- Transient low/flat mood: late-day “flat” affect when infant fussy; single episode of tearfulness with feeding difficulty  
- Occasional sense of being overwhelmed when routine tasks accumulate; resolves with situational change  

Symptoms denied  
- Persistent sadness, hopelessness, or crying spells  
- Sleep-onset or maintenance problems unrelated to infant awakenings  
- Excessive or inappropriate guilt / self-blame  
- Panic attacks or persistent physiological arousal  
- Self-harm or suicidal ideation  

Pattern / screening significance  
Mild, situational mood and anxiety symptoms present; no evidence of major depressive episode or anxiety disorder at this time.  
No current safety concerns. Monitor for symptom escalation, functional impairment, or persistent low mood beyond two weeks.
